analysis.one_liner: Makes it much harder for struggling households to erase credit card and other debts in bankruptcy.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the final weeks of the 106th Congress on October 11, 2000, referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and died there when the Congress ended on January 3, 2001, without ever reaching a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite bankruptcy law to push most individual debtors out of Chapter 7, where unpayable debts are wiped clean, and into Chapter 13, where they must repay creditors from future wages for three to five years. It would do this with a rigid formula (a 'means test') that presumes a debtor is abusing the system if income exceeds IRS expense standards, and it would require debtors to complete paid credit counseling before they could file at all. It bundles in genuine consumer protections — child support moves to the front of the repayment line, creditors who refuse reasonable repayment plans can lose part of their claim, and credit card statements must warn how long minimum payments take — but the core effect shifts money from households in financial distress to their creditors.
analysis.who_benefits: Credit card issuers, consumer lenders, and secured lenders (auto finance, mortgage holders), who would collect billions more from households that today walk away from unpayable debt; credit counseling agencies, which would gain a mandatory pre-filing customer base; and derivatives and securities dealers, whose swap and netting contracts would be exempted from the bankruptcy stay. Custodial parents owed support would gain stronger collection priority.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Credit card issuers and other lenders

how_it_helps.text: Places domestic support obligations — child support and alimony — in the first priority category for repayment, and conditions bankruptcy discharge on the debtor staying current on support owed after filing.

Lets a court cut by up to 20 percent the claim of a creditor that unreasonably refused a reasonable repayment plan proposed through an approved credit counseling agency, and penalizes creditors that willfully fail to credit payments a debtor made.
Requires credit card companies to add minimum-payment warnings and a toll-free number telling cardholders how many years it would take to pay off their balance paying only the minimum.
Protects tax-exempt retirement funds and education savings accounts from being pulled into the bankruptcy estate.
Permanently reenacts Chapter 12 bankruptcy relief for family farmers.

analysis.who_pays: Households filing for bankruptcy. The means test would force many who today qualify for Chapter 7 into multi-year wage garnishment repayment plans; the mandatory counseling and financial-management courses add fees and delay at the moment of crisis; detailed documentation requirements create dismissal traps; and attorneys would face personal liability for filing Chapter 7 cases the formula says are abusive, discouraging legal help for ordinary debtors. The period between Chapter 7 discharges would stretch from six years to eight.

drawbacks.text: The consumer protections in Title II are real: child support claimants gain first priority, and abusive creditor practices draw penalties. A supporter could honestly say those provisions help exactly the low-income households most likely to file.

The costs are concentrated on debtors in genuine distress: formula-based expense allowances set by IRS standards leave little room for real-world costs like childcare or medical needs, and rebutting the presumption of abuse requires itemized documentation and sworn testimony.

Mandatory pre-filing credit counseling adds a fee and a waiting period for every debtor, including those whose circumstances are obvious, and the debtors' attorneys would face fee-shifting and civil penalties if a court later finds the Chapter 7 filing violated the rules — a chilling effect on representation for people with few alternatives.

Longer waiting periods between discharges and tougher reaffirmation rules keep households on the hook for debts longer, reducing the 'fresh start' that bankruptcy law has offered since the 19th century.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is designed so its generous-sounding consumer titles sit alongside a core mechanism — the means test — whose main effect is to route more debtor income to credit card companies and other lenders. The child support and disclosure provisions are worth keeping, but they were available as standalone legislation; here they function as packaging for a measure whose largest financial effect runs toward the credit industry. An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that the counseling mandate, documentation burdens, and attorney-liability provisions raise the price of bankruptcy most for the people least able to pay it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with about twelve weeks left in the Congress, referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day, and no committee ever acted on it before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 — so it never came to any vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Chuck Grassley introduced S. 3186, the Bankruptcy Reform Act of 2000, on October 11, 2000, joined by Sens. Torricelli, Hatch, and Biden as the bill's cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee that same day; the action history records no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action afterward.
The 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, and the bill died in committee without a vote, as legislation does when a new Congress begins and unfinished bills expire.

The core of the bill is a 'needs-based' formula that would presume abuse of Chapter 7 — and force conversion to a repayment plan — for debtors whose income exceeds IRS-based expense standards, replacing the current case-by-case 'substantial abuse' standard.
The same bill would have required every consumer debtor to complete credit counseling before filing and a financial-management course before receiving a discharge.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households in financial distress kept the existing, more accessible bankruptcy system for another Congress; lenders had to wait. The broader campaign for a means test continued and eventually became law in 2005, so the reprieve proved temporary.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumer debtors, for the time being

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, but sponsorship was bipartisan from the start: Grassley and Hatch (Republicans) with Torricelli and Biden (Democrats), and the bill was a continuation of an effort both parties' leaderships had backed in prior Congresses.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and consumer lenders
industries.note: The means test and discharge waiting periods would push households that today erase unpayable card debt into years of court-supervised repayment, transferring billions in expected losses from lenders to debtors. The bill's mandatory counseling and disclosure titles partly offset this by curbing some creditor abuses.

industries.industry: Secured lenders (auto finance and mortgage holders)
industries.note: The bill requires liens on cars and other purchases to survive bankruptcy unless fully paid, and ends the automatic stay quickly when a debtor fails to reaffirm or redeem collateral — meaning debtors can lose vehicles and homes faster.

By barring anyone from filing bankruptcy without an approved nonprofit counseling briefing, the bill makes these agencies the mandatory gateway to bankruptcy relief and creates a nationwide paid market at debtors' expense, though it sets nonprofit and fee standards for approved agencies.

Title IX exempts swap and netting contracts from the bankruptcy stay and limits the trustee's ability to unwind transfers, letting these counterparties exit failed-institution contracts immediately — a benefit paid for by other creditors of the estate.

Title X permanently reenacts Chapter 12 family-farmer bankruptcy relief, which had been repeatedly extended temporarily — a genuine protection for working farm families that runs alongside the bill's lender-friendly core.
